frameworks.name: Magnifying Glass Focus Model
frameworks.definition: Potential and work ethic are analogous to the size of a magnifying glass capturing sunlight; the output (heat/fire) only materializes when focus is concentrated on a single point, regardless of how large the lens is.

frameworks.name: 20% Change-Cost Rule
frameworks.definition: Any business process change produces a guaranteed ~20% temporary decrement in performance before improvement; changes are only justified when the risk-adjusted expected gain exceeds 20% (i.e., a 40%+ improvement with at least 50-50 odds).

frameworks.name: Big List of Ideas
frameworks.definition: A running written list of improvement ideas maintained by the founder, with estimated value and probability attached to each; no idea is acted on immediately — ideas are reviewed later for survivability, and only the highest-ranked ideas are executed when the team has bandwidth.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that dispersing entrepreneurial energy across multiple businesses simultaneously produces a multi-year plateau at the same revenue level that concentrated single-business focus would escape. Hormozi experienced this personally, running nine businesses simultaneously (six gyms, a chiropractor agency, a dental agency, and a turnaround launch business) and reaching only a few million dollars per year — approximately the same revenue as a single-business operator at similar effort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder running multiple businesses simultaneously
Revenue in the low millions range
claims.mechanism: Potential and talent are like a fixed-size magnifying glass; if the lens is not focused on a single point, no output is generated regardless of the lens size.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the more talented a founder is, the more opportunities they can identify that they could pursue — which means the more things they must actively say no to. Talent amplifies the opportunity-cost problem rather than solving it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High-talent founder with multiple viable business options
claims.mechanism: Greater ability to recognize viable opportunities increases the number of tempting alternatives, making focus harder rather than easier for high-talent individuals.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that to make any single business opportunity worth pursuing, a founder must say no to essentially every other opportunity — not just most, but virtually all of them. The price of pursuing everything is that nothing reaches its ceiling.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder with multiple viable opportunities
Goal of building a large-scale business
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders who are satisfied with novelty and variety over scale

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the trade between pursuing novelty across multiple businesses versus committing to one is explicit: multi-business founders get novelty and excitement; single-business founders get scale, systems, and teams. The price of novelty is capped growth; the price of scale is capped variety.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the marketplace reveals the correct business to focus on through purchase behavior: if customers consistently ask to buy a specific offer and not others, that is the signal to concentrate on, not the offers the founder is most excited about internally. He applies this with the heuristic: if three doors exist and customers only knock on one, remove the other two and go all-in on that one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder with multiple offers or business lines
One offer receiving significantly more customer demand than others
claims.mechanism: Customers expressing willingness to pay is the most reliable signal of where value creation is occurring; internal founder excitement is a weaker and often misleading signal.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that any change to a business process — sales scripts, onboarding, leader transitions, training systems — produces a guaranteed approximately 20% temporary decrease in performance before any improvement materializes, because team members carry muscle memory for the old process and require reps to rebuild it under the new one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Any process change in an operating business
Team-dependent businesses (not solo operations)
claims.mechanism: Team members have muscle memory for existing processes; changing the process forces them to rebuild behavioral patterns from scratch, reducing output during the transition period regardless of whether the new process is superior.

numbers.axis: Performance decrement from a business process change

anchors.value: returns to baseline plus the improvement the change was intended to produce

bounded_by: Based on Alex Hormozi's internal Acquisition.com operational experience, not a randomized study
Applies to team-driven process changes; may not apply to purely automated changes with no human adaptation required

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's rule for making any business change is that the expected improvement must be risk-adjusted to exceed 40% at a 50-50 confidence level (equivalent to an expected value of 20%) before the change is worth the guaranteed 20% transition cost. A change expected to produce only a 5% improvement is a bad trade even if that 5% eventually materializes, because it costs a guaranteed 20% loss for months of recovery time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Any operating business with team-dependent processes
Founder or operator evaluating a process change
claims.mechanism: A guaranteed 20% short-term performance loss is the fixed cost of any change; rational change decisions require that the risk-adjusted expected gain exceed this fixed cost.

numbers.axis: Threshold for executing a business process change

anchors.value: 5% improvement at any confidence — does not exceed the 20% guaranteed cost
4-5 months to make up the 20% decrease for a 5% gain

bounded_by: Hormozi's personal threshold derived from Acquisition.com operational experience
Does not apply to changes that can be A/B tested without disrupting the main process

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when left alone without process changes, team members naturally improve at their jobs over time — meaning a founder who avoids premature interventions gets the performance improvement anyway, without paying the 20% transition cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Stable business processes with competent team members
No new process changes introduced
claims.mechanism: Repetition and accumulated experience cause team members to naturally optimize their execution of existing processes, compounding performance without the disruption cost of forced change.

anchors.value: natural ~5% improvement over time as team builds reps
net loss: guaranteed 20% decrease before recovering to the same 5% improvement

claims.text: Alex Hormozi calculates that on the people side of a business, a department can absorb at most one meaningful process change per quarter (approximately four changes per year), not one per week. This is far fewer than entrepreneurs typically assume when they think about testing and iteration.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: People-dependent business processes (sales, onboarding, operations)
Team-based execution requiring retraining and adjustment

numbers.axis: Feasible process change frequency by process type

anchors.value: ~52 tests per year (1 per week), limited by traffic volume requirements
~4 changes per year (1 per quarter) — limited by human adaptation capacity

bounded_by: Automated/digital processes can support higher frequency testing when traffic is sufficient
Assumes each change is a true process change requiring team retraining, not a minor copy tweak

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that most entrepreneurs fail to perceive the true cost of frequent changes because they lack real-time data tracking. Without metrics visible on a short lag (days, not months), the causal link between a process change and subsequent performance decline is invisible — the founder only sees degraded aggregate numbers weeks or months later with no clear attribution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses without real-time operational metrics
Founders using monthly aggregate reporting
claims.mechanism: Monthly aggregated data introduces noise and lag that breaks the feedback loop; the change is made, the performance drops, but the decline appears in data weeks later alongside other variables — making attribution to the specific change impossible.
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses with real-time metric dashboards that make the change-performance relationship visible immediately

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that when he is in writing mode — working on books rather than operating the business — Acquisition.com performs exceptionally well, because the founder's absence from daily business decisions removes the main source of disruptive change.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Mature business with capable teams in place
Founder engaged in a deep creative output channel (writing) that consumes their attention away from operations
claims.mechanism: Founder-initiated process changes are the primary source of disruption in a well-staffed business; when the founder is absorbed elsewhere, the team operates without interruption and compounds naturally.
bounded_by: Requires the business to have a capable team in place — does not apply to early-stage businesses that are genuinely founder-dependent for execution

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends channeling entrepreneurial ADD and creative energy into marketing and content production rather than operational business changes, because marketing benefits from novelty and creative output while operations are harmed by it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder with high creative energy and tendency toward operational tinkering
Business with an established operational team
claims.mechanism: Marketing and content creation are domains that benefit from creativity and novelty output; business operations are domains that are harmed by the same creative impulse applied as process changes.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business owner reaches the realization that they have only a finite number of entrepreneurial seasons — approximately two or three major business builds in a lifetime — which forces ruthless prioritization of which business to commit to and for how long.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Mature founder who has already run multiple businesses or business stages

numbers.axis: Remaining major entrepreneurial builds in a founder's career

anchors.region: Alex Hormozi's personal assessment at time of recording

anchors.value: single business (Acquisition.com) until unable to continue

bounded_by: Hormozi's anecdotal self-assessment; not a studied population figure

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the vast majority of entrepreneurs making changes frequently to their businesses never identify what actually caused a performance decline, because they change too many things too often — destroying the ability to attribute outcomes to specific interventions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Entrepreneurs who make multiple simultaneous process changes
Businesses without real-time isolated testing
claims.mechanism: When multiple changes are made simultaneously, the causal chain between any individual change and its performance effect is broken — the experimenter cannot isolate which variable produced the outcome.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses Warren Buffett's punch card investing model as an analogy for business process changes: if founders operated as if they only had a punch card allowing 20 lifetime investments, they would be far more selective and deliberate — applying the same logic to process changes would produce significantly better business outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Entrepreneurs evaluating whether to make a process change

numbers.axis: Process change frequency analogy to investment decisions

anchors.value: 20 investments in a lifetime — forces extreme selectivity

anchors.region: Hormozi's applied equivalent for large businesses
anchors.value: fewer than 4 process changes per year per department

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes his own experience running nine businesses simultaneously — six gyms, a chiropractor agency, a dental agency, and a turnaround launch business doing done-for-you sales — while generating approximately the same revenue as Kira (a few million dollars per year). He uses this personal plateau as evidence that multi-business dispersion caps revenue growth regardless of total effort invested.

Kira (the business owner being advised) describes closing $1.25 million in five minutes at a live event in January from a crowd of 30, operating a publishing house, running luxury 5-day book-writing adventures (one week per month), renting an island in the British Virgin Islands for 15 people, hosting a TV show, and running a business school for women — all simultaneously as a single mother of five. Despite this activity, she reports being on track for $4 million with aspirations for $10 million, but feeling spread thin and overwhelmed with no clarity on direction. Alex Hormozi identifies that Kira's customers consistently come to her for books, not for the business school — suggesting this is the marketplace signal she should follow.

Alex Hormozi describes the mechanism of his Big List of Ideas: whenever he generates a new business improvement idea, instead of calling an emergency team meeting, he writes it down and continues living his life. When an idea survives 30 days of reflection and still seems valuable, he brings it to the team with his reasoning. The team then compares it against all other 40-50% return ideas already on the list to rank-order by expected value and likelihood. Only when the team has bandwidth does he execute the highest-ranked idea.

Alex Hormozi describes observing performance decrements at Acquisition.com's advisory practice whenever any process change is made — whether in sales scripting, onboarding, or team transitions. Even when confident the change is superior, he observes a performance decrease before the improvement materializes. This consistent pattern across multiple departments and change types is what led him to formalize the 20% decrement rule and the 40% risk-adjusted threshold for making any change.

practices.text: Channel creative and ADD energy into marketing and content production — specifically lead magnets, ads, and books — rather than into operational or process changes inside the business.

Maintain a written list of all business improvement ideas on your phone. Do not act on ideas immediately. Assign an estimated improvement value and likelihood to each. Sleep on ideas for at least two to four weeks before evaluating them seriously. Only surface ideas to the team when you have sufficient bandwidth and the idea still seems compelling after the waiting period.

Before executing any business process change, explicitly calculate whether the risk-adjusted expected improvement exceeds 20%. If the expected gain (improvement percentage times probability of success) does not exceed 20%, do not make the change.

Install real-time operational metrics (NPS, ascension rates, churn, conversion rates) with short feedback lags so that the performance impact of any process change is visible within days, not months. This makes the cost of change visible and prevents invisible attribution errors.
When multiple customers consistently come to you asking to buy the same thing, follow that signal. Remove other offers and doors. Go all-in on the offer the marketplace is already selecting.
